metadata.title: A Stochastic Gradient Method with an Exponential Convergence Rate for Finite Training Sets (Le Roux, Schmidt, Bach, 2012)
metadata.framework: Stochastic Average Gradient (SAG): variance-reduced stochastic gradient method achieving linear convergence for finite-sum strongly convex optimization
metadata.source_note: Extraction based on arXiv:1202.6258 PDF text.

nodes.name: Finite-sum optimization problem
nodes.statement: Minimize $f(x) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} f_i(x)$ where each $f_i$ is a smooth (Lipschitz-continuous gradient) convex function and $f$ is strongly convex. This arises in empirical risk minimization with $n$ training examples.

nodes.name: Stochastic Average Gradient (SAG) algorithm
nodes.statement: Maintain a table of $n$ gradient values $y_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$, one per component function $f_i$. At each iteration: (1) Sample $i_t$ uniformly from $\{1, \ldots, n\}$. (2) Update $y_{i_t} \leftarrow \nabla f_{i_t}(x_t)$ (refresh only the sampled gradient). (3) Update $x_{t+1} = x_t - \frac{\alpha}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i$. The direction is the average of the most recent gradient for each $f_i$.

nodes.name: Strong convexity constant
nodes.statement: The function $f$ is $\mu$-strongly convex if $f(y) \geq f(x) + \nabla f(x)^T(y-x) + \frac{\mu}{2}\|y-x\|^2$ for all $x, y$. The condition number is $\kappa = L/\mu$ where $L$ is the Lipschitz constant of $\nabla f$.

nodes.name: Linear convergence rate of SAG
nodes.statement: With step size $\alpha = \frac{1}{16L}$, SAG achieves $\mathbb{E}[f(x_t) - f(x^*)] \leq C \cdot \rho^t$ where $\rho = 1 - \min\left(\frac{1}{8n}, \frac{\mu}{16L}\right)$ and $C$ depends on $\|x_0 - x^*\|^2$ and initial gradient errors. This is a linear (exponential) convergence rate, contrasting with the $O(1/t)$ sublinear rate of standard SGD.

nodes.name: Variance reduction property
nodes.statement: As $x_t \to x^*$, the variance of the SAG gradient estimate goes to zero (because all stored gradients $y_i$ converge to $\nabla f_i(x^*)$, and the average gradient at the optimum is zero for the full gradient). This is in contrast to SGD, where gradient variance remains nonzero at the optimum.

nodes.name: Memory requirement
nodes.statement: SAG requires $O(nd)$ memory to store $n$ gradient vectors of dimension $d$. For sparse problems (e.g., generalized linear models), only the non-zero entries need to be stored, reducing this to $O(\mathrm{nnz})$ where $\mathrm{nnz}$ is the total number of non-zeros in the data.

nodes.name: Biased gradient estimate
nodes.statement: Unlike standard SGD, the SAG gradient estimate is biased: $\mathbb{E}[\frac{1}{n}\sum_i y_i] \neq \nabla f(x_t)$ because the stored gradients $y_i$ were computed at different past iterates. Despite this bias, the method converges linearly because the bias vanishes as the iterates converge.

nodes.name: Comparison with full gradient and SGD
nodes.statement: SAG combines the advantages of both methods: it has the low per-iteration cost of SGD ($O(d)$ per step) and the linear convergence rate of full gradient descent. The total cost to reach $\epsilon$-accuracy is $O((n + \kappa) \log(1/\epsilon))$, compared to $O(n\kappa \log(1/\epsilon))$ for GD and $O(\kappa^2/\epsilon)$ for SGD.
